MEMORY: I asked Ambrose straight what ailed the children and the clock. He wanted no coin, which sat odd with me. He said once in a hundred years the clock tries to strike thirteen at midnight, and a road opens and takes what's waiting in town. I must jam something iron, a poker, in the Great Gear before midnight, since he can't climb the ladder. Down in the Lopsided Square I faced the peddler Tibbersnatch. He holds Pip's brother Tod's shadow and seven other children's in a jar. He'd trade the lot for a tin whistle, old, loved fifty years, tune worn soft. Mags has no whistle. Pip says it's old Mr. Tock's, played every sunset up in the clock tower, and she asked if I'd help or just stand there.

LEARNED: Every hearth in Wumbleby has a poker, and iron is what I need to jam the Great Gear.
LEARNED: The Great Gear is up in the gearloft of the Tock Tower, and Ambrose can't climb the ladder any more.
LEARNED: Once in a hundred years the clock tries to strike thirteen at midnight, and a road opens that takes whatever is waiting in town.
LEARNED: The clock has run fast for three days, since the peddler Tibbersnatch came.
LEARNED: Ambrose asked no coin for his help.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch keeps the stolen shadows in a jar, and they travel with him at midnight.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch will give up the jar for a tin whistle, old, loved fifty years, with its tune worn soft.
LEARNED: Mags Ragwort has no whistle and sells nothing, only rags and bones.
LEARNED: Pip says the whistle is old Mr. Tock's, played every sunset in the clock tower.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch took Tod's shadow and seven other children's, and Pip wants them back before midnight.

MEMORY: I asked old Ambrose what ails the children, and he took no coin for it. He said the clock tries to strike thirteen once in a hundred years, and a road opens and takes what's waiting in town. Jam iron in the Great Gear's teeth before midnight and it won't strike. Every hearth has a poker, and he can't climb the ladder any more. I went down to the Lopsided Square and faced the peddler, Tibbersnatch. He keeps the shadows in a jar and will trade the lot for a tin whistle, old, loved fifty years, tune worn soft. Mags has no whistle. Pip says it's old Mr. Tock's, up in the clock tower, played every sunset. She asked whether I'd help or just stand there like the other grown-ups. I haven't answered her yet.

LEARNED: The clock tries to strike thirteen at midnight once in a hundred years, and a road opens and takes what's waiting in town.
LEARNED: Jamming iron, not wood, in the teeth of the Great Gear in the gearloft before midnight stops the thirteenth stroke.
LEARNED: Every hearth in town has a poker, and Ambrose has no iron bar.
LEARNED: Ambrose can't climb the ladder to the gearloft any more.
LEARNED: Ambrose took no coin for what he told me.
LEARNED: The peddler Tibbersnatch came three days ago, and the clock has run fast since.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch keeps the stolen shadows in a jar and takes them away at midnight.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch will give up the jar for a tin whistle, old and loved fifty years, with a tune worn soft.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch took Tod's shadow and seven other children's.
LEARNED: Mags Ragwort sells nothing and has no whistle.
LEARNED: The whistle is old Mr. Tock's, in the clock tower, played every sunset (Pip says).
LEARNED: Pip Pumbleton wants the shadows back before midnight and carries a cricket bat.

MEMORY: I asked Ambrose about the clock, and he took no coin for it. He said that once in a hundred years the clock tries to strike thirteen at midnight, and a road opens and takes whatever waits in town. It's been ticking fast three days, since the peddler came. Iron jammed in the Great Gear's teeth will stop it, and a hearth poker would do. Ambrose can't climb the ladder any more. I went down to the Lopsided Square and faced the peddler, Tibbersnatch. He keeps the children's shadows in a jar and will trade them for a tin whistle, old and loved fifty years. Mags has no whistle. Pip says it's old Mr. Tock's, up in the clock tower, and he plays it every sunset. She asked if I'd help or just stand there like the other grown-ups. Fair's fair, and I haven't answered her yet.

LEARNED: The Wumbleby clock tries to strike thirteen at midnight once in a hundred years, and a road opens out of the world and takes what's waiting in town.
LEARNED: Ambrose says to jam something stout and iron, not wood, in the Great Gear's teeth in the gearloft before midnight, and the clock will never strike thirteen.
LEARNED: Every hearth in town has a poker, and Ambrose has no iron bar of his own.
LEARNED: Ambrose can't climb the ladder to the gearloft any more.
LEARNED: Ambrose asked no coin for what he told me.
LEARNED: The clock has been ticking fast for three days, since the peddler came.
LEARNED: Mister Tibbersnatch, the peddler, keeps the shadows in a jar and takes it with him at midnight.
LEARNED: Tibbersnatch will trade the whole jar of shadows for a tin whistle, old, loved fifty years, with its tune worn soft.
LEARNED: He took Tod's shadow and seven other children's.
LEARNED: Mags Ragwort buys rags and bones and sells nothing, and she has no whistle.
LEARNED: The whistle is old Mr. Tock's, up in the clock tower, and he plays it every sunset, according to Pip.
LEARNED: Pip Pumbleton wants the shadows back before midnight and carries a cricket bat.

MEMORY: Goodness, what a night! I couldn't sleep, so I went out in my one good shawl and found Pip Pumbleton on the fountain rim with a cricket bat, three nights awake, her brother Tod fast asleep since he wound a tin rabbit from the peddler. Seven other children too. Mags Ragwort swore she'd never touch a peddler's toy, because nothing's free, and pointed me down Crooked Lane where small shadows walk by themselves. I said I'd help Pip, and Dilly and Hester came along with their pole and poker. We passed a grating that licks and whispers rhymes, and I wouldn't answer it. At the bottom was Gloomer's Meadow and the striped wagon with its keyhole door, shadows queuing up the steps like a church line. Hester peeked in. No peddler, only a jar of grey stuff breathing on a table. She wants the three of us to go in together before he comes back, and it's near midnight.

LEARNED: Pip's brother Tod has slept since winding a tin rabbit the peddler gave him, three days ago, and seven other children sleep too.
LEARNED: The children's shadows get up at night and walk down Crooked Lane to the striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow.
LEARNED: The striped wagon is red and white, with a crooked chimney, a lantern over the door, and a keyhole-shaped door; it smells of tin and peppermint.
LEARNED: Inside the wagon, on a table, is a glass jar of grey stuff that turns as if breathing; it is likely where the shadows or the sleep are kept.
LEARNED: A lullaby that never finishes its tune hums from the wagon.
LEARNED: A round iron grating in Crooked Lane has something licking beneath it that whispers rhymes and wants someone to answer.
LEARNED: Mags Ragwort says she never took the peddler's toys, and that nothing free is really free.
LEARNED: The peddler sings "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" and carries a humming tray of tin things.
LEARNED: Dilly Quickstep carries a lamplighter's pole and Hester Gimbal an iron poker; both are helping me.
LEARNED: I carry my Silver Thimble in my pocket.

MEMORY: Goodness, what a night. I couldn't sleep, so I went out in my good shawl, and found Pip Pumbleton on the fountain's rim with a cricket bat, gone grey with worry. Her brother Tod wound a tin rabbit from the peddler and fell asleep smiling, and seven other children with him. Mags Ragwort swore she'd never touched the peddler's toys and said small shadows walk down Crooked Lane at night. I told Pip I'd help, and we went down with Dilly and her lamplighter's pole, and Hester Gimbal joined us with her iron poker and her notebook. Halfway down, the drain-grating whispered rhymes and licked wet, and I wouldn't let anyone answer it. At Gloomer's Meadow we found the red-and-white striped wagon with its keyhole door, the lullaby humming, and the shadows queuing to slip in one by one. Hester peeked and saw no peddler, only a glass jar of grey stuff turning as if it breathed. Now we're about to go in together for a proper look before he comes back, and before midnight. I'd dearly love the children awake and everyone looking at me twice for it.

LEARNED: Pip's brother Tod and seven other children fell asleep after winding the peddler's tin toys and haven't woken.
LEARNED: At night the children's shadows leave the walls, walk down Crooked Lane and go into the striped wagon through its keyhole door.
LEARNED: The striped red-and-white wagon stands in Gloomer's Meadow at the bottom of Crooked Lane, and smells of tin and peppermint.
LEARNED: Inside the wagon is a glass jar of grey stuff that turns as if breathing; Pip and Hester both saw it and think the shadows or the sleep are kept there.
LEARNED: The peddler was not in the wagon when Hester looked, and he sings "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" somewhere nearby.
LEARNED: A drain-grating halfway down Crooked Lane whispers rhymes and wants someone to answer; it only licks patiently when ignored, so I don't answer it.
LEARNED: Mags Ragwort says she never took any peddler's toys because nothing free is really free, and her cart holds only rags, bones and bottles.
LEARNED: Dilly Quickstep carries a lamplighter's pole and Hester Gimbal carries an iron poker and a notebook; both are with me.
LEARNED: Pip Pumbleton says it must be done before midnight.

MEMORY: Goodness, what a night it's been, and me in my one good shawl! I went to the Lopsided Square because I couldn't sleep, and it turned into the busiest sort of night. Pip Pumbleton, rumpled as a pillowcase and clutching her cricket bat, told me the peddler's tin rabbit sent her brother Tod and seven other children to sleep, and that their shadows get up at night and walk down Crooked Lane to a striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow. She'd seen a big jar of grey stuff in there. Mags Ragwort swore she'd never taken a toy from the peddler ("nothing's free, somebody's paying") but admitted she'd seen small shadows walking and kept her lantern lit and didn't look. I said I'd help, and Dilly Quickstep came along with her lamplighter's pole and Hester Gimbal with her iron poker and notebook. On the lane we passed a drain grating that licked and whispered a rhyme asking who'd answer. Dilly poked it, and I said we should leave it be and not answer. We followed the trotting shadows to the meadow and the striped wagon with the keyhole door and a lullaby that never quite finishes. Hester peeked through the door and says the peddler's out, but a jar of grey stuff sits on the table, turning as if it breathes. Now she wants the three of us to go in together while Dilly holds the pole across the door and I keep watch. I'd still love to be the one who gets the children's shadows back, and have all of Wumbleby look at me twice for it.

LEARNED: The peddler's wind-up toys, like the tin rabbit, put children into a sleep they don't wake from; Tod and seven other children are asleep.
LEARNED: At night the sleeping children's shadows leave and walk down Crooked Lane to the peddler's wagon.
LEARNED: The peddler's wagon is red and white striped, stands in Gloomer's Meadow, and has a keyhole-shaped door, a crooked chimney and a lantern over the door.
LEARNED: A glass jar of grey stuff that turns as if breathing sits on the table inside the wagon; Pip and Hester both saw it, and it is probably where the shadows or the sleep are kept.
LEARNED: The peddler was not in the wagon when Hester looked, and he calls out "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" while his tray of tin toys hums.
LEARNED: A round iron grating in Crooked Lane makes a wet licking sound and whispers a rhyme asking who will answer; nothing has come up through it, and it is best left unanswered.
LEARNED: Mags Ragwort says she never takes the peddler's free toys because nothing is free, and she keeps her lantern lit and doesn't look at the shadows.
LEARNED: Pip Pumbleton wants her brother Tod's shadow back and has not slept in three nights.
LEARNED: Hester Gimbal, Dilly Quickstep and Pip are on my side; Dilly has a lamplighter's pole and Hester an iron poker.
LEARNED: I carry a Silver Thimble in my pocket.

MEMORY: I went asking Mags, chum, what the peddler's toys cost and what was left of them. She said she never took one, "nothing's free, somebody's paying," and that she's watched small shadows walk down Crooked Lane at night on their own, and she doesn't look. Then Pip told it plain: her brother Tod wound a tin rabbit three days back and fell asleep smiling, seven other children too, and their shadows go off to a striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow where there's a big jar of grey stuff. Marigold called me to light the way, so I took my pole and went down Crooked Lane with her and Hester. The grating in the gutter whispered a rhyme when I poked it, and Marigold said not to answer it, so we left it licking. The others went on ahead and I hurried after, calling for them to wait. At the meadow the wagon stood with its door ajar, no peddler in sight, a line of shadows waiting at the steps. Hester saw the jar on the table, grey stuff turning like it breathes, shadows slipping in by the keyhole. She wants me to hold the pole across the door while we go in together for a proper look before he comes back.

LEARNED: The peddler's tin wind-up toys put the children to sleep; Tod wound a tin rabbit three days ago and eight children now sleep.
LEARNED: The sleepers' shadows get up at night and walk down Crooked Lane to the striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow.
LEARNED: Crooked Lane runs south from the Lopsided Square down to Gloomer's Meadow.
LEARNED: A glass jar of grey stuff that turns as if breathing sits on the table inside the striped wagon; the shadows go in by the keyhole.
LEARNED: Mags never took a toy from the peddler and says nothing's free; she keeps her lantern burning and doesn't look at the shadows.
LEARNED: A round grating in Crooked Lane's gutter licks and whispers a rhyme; Marigold says not to answer it.
LEARNED: Marigold Thimble and Hester Gimbal are helping, and Hester carries a notebook and an iron poker.
LEARNED: Pip Pumbleton is the sleeping Tod's sister and wants something done before midnight.

MEMORY: Fascinating night! I listened at the drain on Crooked Lane and something under the grating giggled a rhyme at me and called me rude when I snatched up the little iron poker. Marigold and Dilly came after me, and we followed the small shadows trotting downhill with no children attached, all the way to Gloomer's Meadow. There stood a red-and-white striped wagon with a keyhole door, and the shadows queued up to slip inside it politely. I peeked through the gap and saw a glass jar of grey stuff turning as if it breathed, and no peddler in sight. I told Marigold and Dilly what I saw, and we agreed to go in together and take a proper look at that jar before he comes back.

LEARNED: The drain-grating in Crooked Lane has a licking, rhyming voice beneath it that giggles "Again and again!" and calls me rude if I answer it.
LEARNED: The sleeping children's shadows are leaving them and trotting south down Crooked Lane toward Gloomer's Meadow.
LEARNED: In Gloomer's Meadow stands a tall red-and-white striped wagon with a crooked chimney and a keyhole-shaped door, smelling of tin and peppermint, with a lullaby humming inside.
LEARNED: The shadows queue at the wagon steps and slip in through the keyhole one at a time.
LEARNED: On a table inside the wagon sits a glass jar of grey stuff that turns slowly as if breathing; I think it holds the sleep or the shadows.
LEARNED: A toy peddler calls "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" nearby with a humming tray of tin things; he is probably the wagon's owner and was away from it.
LEARNED: I carry an iron poker, taken from the gutter by the drain, and my notebook.
LEARNED: Marigold Thimble and Dilly Quickstep (who carries the lamplighter's pole and a lamp) are with me and want to hunt this together; Marigold asked me not to go in without her.

MEMORY: Fascinating night! I listened at the drain on Crooked Lane and something down there giggled a rhyme at me, and when I answered it, it only sulked "Rude." Then I saw small shadows trotting downhill with no children attached, so I took the little iron poker from the gutter and Marigold and Dilly joined me. We followed the shadows south into Gloomer's Meadow, where a red-and-white striped wagon stood with a lullaby humming inside. The shadows queue up politely and slip in through the keyhole door. I peeked in and saw no peddler, only a glass jar of grey stuff turning as if it were breathing. I promised Marigold I wouldn't go in alone, so I told them both what I saw, and we mean to go in together for a proper look before the peddler comes back.

LEARNED: A red-and-white striped wagon with a crooked chimney and a keyhole-shaped door stands in Gloomer's Meadow, and the shadows queue to slip inside it.
LEARNED: A glass jar of grey stuff turns like it is breathing on a table inside the wagon, and I suspect it holds the sleep, the shadows, or both.
LEARNED: A toy peddler calls "Toys for the little ones!" nearby, and the wagon smells of tin and peppermint, so I suspect he is behind the stolen shadows.
LEARNED: The drain grating halfway down Crooked Lane licks its lips, rhymes, giggles, and sulks if answered rudely, but it has told me nothing useful.
LEARNED: I carry an iron poker taken from the gutter by the drain, and my notebook.
LEARNED: Marigold Thimble and Dilly Quickstep are helping me, and Dilly carries the lamplighter's pole and a lamp.
LEARNED: I promised Marigold that I would tell her what I saw and not go into the wagon without her.

MEMORY: Fascinating night! I put my ear to that grating on Crooked Lane and it whispered a rhyme at me, "who will answer me, once again?", and giggled when my answer went down it. Rude, it called me, too. I took the little iron poker from the gutter and caught Marigold up. Then we followed the loose shadows, trotting along with no children attached, south into Gloomer's Meadow. Dilly came along with the lamplighter's pole. In the meadow stands a red-and-white striped wagon with a lullaby humming inside, and a patient line of shadows queuing up its steps and slipping through the keyhole door. I peeked through the gap and saw a glass jar of grey stuff turning as if it breathed, with no peddler in sight. I promised Marigold I'd tell her before going in, so I told them both, and we meant to go in together for a proper look at that jar.

LEARNED: The round iron drain-grating halfway down Crooked Lane whispers rhymes ("Down in the dark where the drippings drain, who will answer me, once again?") and licks its lips, and it does not like being answered or being called rude.
LEARNED: Answering the drain's rhyme is a bad idea; Marigold advised leaving it to its licking.
LEARNED: The children's missing shadows trot down Crooked Lane toward Gloomer's Meadow with nobody attached.
LEARNED: In Gloomer's Meadow stands a tall red-and-white striped wagon with a crooked chimney, a lantern, and a keyhole-shaped door that stands a little open; it smells of tin and peppermint, and a lullaby hums from it that never finishes its tune.
LEARNED: The shadows queue up at the wagon steps and slip in through the keyhole one by one.
LEARNED: Inside the wagon, on a table, sits a glass jar of grey stuff that turns slowly as if breathing; I suspect it holds the sleep or the shadows.
LEARNED: A peddler calls "Toys! Toys for the little ones!" with a tray of humming tin toys; he was not at the wagon when I looked, and I suspect he is behind the shadow-taking.
LEARNED: I carry an iron poker taken from the gutter near the drain, and my notebook.
LEARNED: Marigold Thimble is brave and careful, tends to walk ahead, and made me promise not to go into the wagon without her.
LEARNED: Dilly Quickstep carries a lamplighter's pole, is loyal, and follows to keep Marigold and me safe.
